content:Speaker user says: How can elementary students create their own character poem using Roald Dahl's poetry as an example?: Students will enjoy analyzing the exuberant poems of Roald Dahl. His creative rhymes are an intrinsic part of his classic stories. They add a wacky break in the story line, while giving insight into the character or situation at hand. Roald Dahl poems pepper his books such as; The Witches, Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and James and the Giant Peach play an integral part in the stories.
Roald Dahl was very kind to English teachers when he wrote the many lines of verse. His poetry follows classic patterns, making it easy to incorporate his works into any study of poetry.
For this lesson, I used the book Vile Verses, an anthology of Roald Dahl’s poetry from his books, as well as poems that were previously unpublished. He was a prolific writer who also retold nursery rhymes and described animals with a very different point of view.
For this two part study for elementary students, wake the students up by reciting, Down With Children from The Witches. This silly poem is a fantastic way to get their attention and teach the concept of rhyming couplets.
Couplets are made up of two lines. At the end of the lines are words that rhyme and the two lines together make a complete thought.
Have the students pick out the rhyming couplets that Roald Dahl used; in, skin, mash, bash, louder, powder, trice, mice and so on.
Ask the class to brainstorm their own collection of rhyming words. Keeping a running list in a poetry notebook is a good idea for future lessons.
Work on a building a piece of poetry using couplets that the students come up with.
Once the class gets the concept of rhyming couplets down, introduce another Roald Dahl poem such as this one from Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Concerning Veronica Salt.This poem also makes good use of rhyming couplets and can be used as another excellent example, although for this lesson focus on Character poetry.
Start by breaking the students into work groups of four or five.
Recite the poem to the class, have handouts of the poem, if possible, to give to each group.
Let them pick out the rhyming words in this poem and copy into their poetry notebook as a reference. Have the groups share the rhyming words they have previously come up with as well.
Now, invite the groups to come up with a character.
They will start by deciding if it will be a boy or girl, man or woman.
What are the faults of this person? Describe them with lots of expression.
Exaggerate how they look, talk and walk.
How do they like to spend their time?
One of the students from each group can be the designated artist and draw the character as it is described.
Have the groups put their thoughts together into couplets individually.
Then let them string the couplets together to create a unique character poem.
Roald Dahl poems will get reluctant writers to the page. Try incorporating his verse whenever your lessons start to get a little stale and watch the class perk up. context:Charlie and the Chocolate Factory keywords: Roald Dahl, poetry, character, rhyme, student, lesson, creative writing, poem, analysis, elementary, classroom tags: Poetry, Character Development, Rhyme, Creative Writing, Analysis, Roald Dahl, Literature, Group Work, Poetry Analysis

content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Here are some tips on how to help students come up with descriptive language for their character poems:

2. Use the senses: Encourage students to use sensory details in their character poems. For example, they could describe how their character smells, sounds, tastes, looks, and feels.

content:Speaker assistant says: That's a great skill to pass on to your grandchildren! Here are some tips on how to make gardening fun and engaging for them:

1. Involve them in the planning: Let your grandchildren help plan the garden, including selecting which vegetables to grow, where to plant them, and what supplies they'll need. Allow them to take ownership of the project and make decisions for themselves.

2. Make it hands-on: Children love to get their hands dirty! Encourage your grandchildren to actively participate in the planting and care of the garden. You can assign them tasks that are age-appropriate, such as watering or pulling weeds.

3. Teach them about the plants: Explain to your grandchildren the life cycle of plants, the importance of soil, and the role of the sun, water, and air in plant growth. You can also introduce them to the insects and worms that live in the soil.

4. Play gardening games: Make the experience fun by playing games, such as "I spy" with garden objects, "Simon says" with gardening instructions, or a treasure hunt to find hidden treasures in the garden.

5. Reward them: Encourage your grandchildren by rewarding them for their hard work, such as allowing them to pick the first ripe vegetable or creating a prize for the biggest or most unique vegetable.

By making gardening a fun and interactive experience, your grandchildren will not only learn a valuable skill, but also develop a love and appreciation for nature. context:new context keywords: gardening, grandchildren, skills, plants tags: reward, gardening, grandchildren, skills, plants, growing, rewarding, garden, community, connection

content:Speaker assistant says: Chef William had always been up for a culinary challenge. He saw cooking as an art form, an ability to create something awe-inspiring from almost anything. So when he found himself stranded on a remote island, with no survival gear or supplies, the idea of making a delicious meal became top on his list.

The Island was like no other he had ever seen. Thick canopies of trees with an overgrowth of vines made it hard to cut through. The sand was greyish brown, compared to the white sand beaches he was used to, and the water was a deep green color, almost opaque.

As he explored the island along the beach, he found strange and unfamiliar ingredients that only the rainforest could give. He couldn't believe his luck. Many of the ingredients he encountered he had only read about in culinary books but had never tasted or cooked with.

With no cooking supplies, William improvised. He started by building a makeshift kitchen, with a few rocks as his stove and a wooden platform as his counter. It wasn't much, but he made it work. He used the rocks to heat up coconut oil, which he mixed with wild herbs he'd foraged to create a fragrant and delicious flavor base.

The limited resources on the island presented an added challenge. There were no knives, no cutting boards, and no utensils to cook with, so William had to be resourceful. He used a large rock he found as a knife, and a slab of wood as a cutting board.

He experimented with the ingredients he found on the island, and soon he realized he was onto something. He discovered that the tangy fruit he had picked was great with the fish he had caught earlier, and he found a spicy root that was perfect for the soup he was cooking.

Days went by, and William's creativity with the new and unfamiliar ingredients grew. He made an array of dishes; roasted fruits and vegetables, fish, soups and stews, all from scratch and without any of his usual kitchen utensils. He even caught fish himself, used leaves as plates and rustled up something he never thought was possible: a dessert made of grated coconut, roasted wild fruits and tree sap.

Though he was miles away from civilization and everything he knew, William was happy. He realized that he had found a new kind of satisfaction in cooking, one that came from exploring and discovering new flavors and cooking techniques.

After weeks of experimentation, William got picked up by a passing cruise ship. On the long journey home, he thought back on the adventure he had just finished. content:Speaker user says: How can you make a healthy soup more flavorful without adding unhealthy ingredients?: People are starting to try and eat healthier these days; sadly many people dont have the first idea on where to start or what to do to succeed in this. Eating soup is always a good idea if you want to become a healthier person. Some soups arent really a good idea to eat if you want to be healthy, but many really are. Healthy soup recipes are always a good thing to try and find, they can be filling and good for you when utilizing the correct ingredients.
The first thing that you need to know is that when using vegetables in a soup, make sure that you get fresh ones. Fresh ones are the best for you, however if you cant get fresh to use then try frozen. Frozen is the next best thing for you. Canned is always the worst for you. Try to avoid eating canned vegetables unless you absolutely have to. Despite this, canned beans and pulses are good if you dont want to soak dried ones, as they do save a lot of time. Remember, nothing beats fresh produce.
Although most associated broths and light soups with weight loss, many soups that are good for you are thicker and more wholesome. Many heavy soups use cream, and this should be avoided. Cream can be very fatty and thus very bad for you. A good way to make sure that your soup is healthy is by using milk instead of cream. Milk is better for you and if you can use skimmed milk then that is even better. Dont shy away from thick, hearty soups (just make sure to avoid cream, butter, and other fatty ingredients).
If you find that your healthy soups are slightly tasteless, then why not try and add more herbs and spices to the soup. Many people will tend to add more bad ingredients to a soup to make it taste more to their liking. This is okay to an extent, but if you do that too much then what you will end up with is a calorie filled soup. That is not the ultimate goal. Try to use low calorie and low fat ingredients in your soups to add flavor. This will ensure they are perfect for helping you to lose weight.

content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Here are some healthy and filling soup recipes that you can try at home:

1. Lentil Soup:  Lentils are packed with protein and fiber, making them a great choice for a filling soup. You can add some diced carrots, celery, onion, and garlic to the lentils, and season with cumin, oregano, and smoked paprika. You can also add some spinach or kale at the end for extra nutrition.

2. Vegetable Soup: Vegetable soup is a classic and always a great option for a healthy and filling meal. You can use any vegetables you like, such as carrots, celery, onion, garlic, broccoli, cauliflower, zucchini, and tomatoes. Herbs like thyme, rosemary, and bay leaves add a lovely flavor, but be sure to avoid any cream-based broths.

3. Chicken Noodle Soup: This classic soup is still a great choice for a healthy and filling meal. You can use chicken breast, chopped carrots, celery, onions, garlic, and a sprinkle of thyme. Add some egg noodles towards the end of cooking for a warm and comforting meal.

4. Butternut Squash Soup: Butternut squash is another great ingredient to use for a creamy soup that is still healthy and filling. Roast your butternut squash along with some onions, carrots, and garlic. Add some vegetable broth, nutmeg, and cinnamon, and blend until smooth.

5. Tortilla Soup:  Tortilla soup is a Mexican-inspired soup that is spicy and filling. Use diced onions, garlic, jalapeño peppers, and diced tomatoes. Add some cumin, chili powder, and paprika for flavor. You can add chicken, beans, and tortilla strips to make it more filling. 

These are just some examples of healthy and filling soups that you can easily make at home. Remember, you can always modify the recipes to suit your personal preferences, but be sure to choose low-calorie and nutrient-dense ingredients to keep your soups healthy and filling. content:Speaker user says: When I left college I thought I was a pretty good cook. I had a repertoire of Mid-West inspired meals at my fingertips that I grew up with: Spaghetti, Chili Pie, Quiche Lorraine, Teriyaki Chicken and Rice (my homage to Asia: no veggies, just chicken breast chunks, Yoshida’s and Uncle Ben’s 5 minute rice). Add to that the frozen meals from Trader Joe’s that I could quickly heat on the stove or in the microwave and you have a pretty good idea of what I would eat in a given week. The first inkling I had that there was more to at-home cooking than bland, quick and easy-to-make meals was when I would eat with my post-college boyfriend (my now-husband) and his medical school roommates. They didn’t use recipes and certainly didn’t read instructions the rare times they used anything pre-made. Nic, AJ and Chris would throw things from the fridge directly into a big pan, and would then create some sort of sauce to go with it from whatever liquids they had on hand. They used herbs, REAL garlic (up to this point I thought garlic was a powder that you would buy in the spice aisle), and all manners of fresh vegetables. It was inspired chaos and it was delicious. I loved the by-product of these kitchen sessions, but their cooking methods really stressed me out. If I didn’t know how to cook a meal by heart, I would HAVE to have instructions and would HAVE to follow them step-by-step. It dawned on me that if I had skills, knowledge, and confidence in my cooking abilities I’d be able to cook more freely. So I began to take cooking classes. The beauty of cooking classes is that you learn a whole host of skills while enjoying delicious food and unique cocktails. It ends up being just a really fun, educational experience. I took my first classes in San Diego in Pacific Beach at Great News. I took observational classes, where the chef prepares the meal while teaching knife skills, cooking techniques, shortcuts, and easy variations to the recipes they shared. In San Francisco there are several cooking schools that are highly recommended. I took a page from Julia Child and took my first class in SOMA at Le Cordon Bleu. Le Cordon Bleu is a professional cooking school but they also offer classes for non-professionals. My husband and I took a “Home for the Holidays” class the weekend before Thanksgiving so that we were prepared to host our first Thanksgiving meal. This was the first hands-on class I have taken and I really enjoyed it. The Chef started us off by teaching the preparation of the main dish, Turkey Ballentine. Then we all went to stations and prepared the other side dishes for the meal. We were stuck chopping and peeling vegetables for the Ginger Apple Butternut Squash Bisque for a bit at our station, but as soon as we finished we were able to follow the chef around station by station and learned knife skills, cooking chemistry, and helpful tricks. At the end of the morning we all sat down and enjoyed the Thanksgiving feast we had each played a part in. We were also able to take home some of the incredible Turkey Giblet Gravy that the chef himself had whipped up out of a home-made turkey stock, roux, and a savory mixture of herbs. ~ by jessicamoriates on December 5, 2010. content:Speaker assistant says: One summer, I decided to take a solo trip to South Africa. As soon as I stepped off the plane, I was hit by the bright, hot sun and the intense energy of the city of Johannesburg. My preconceptions of South Africa as a strife-ridden, poverty-stricken country were immediately challenged by the vibrant, bustling streets and colorful markets. I quickly realized that my experience was going to be far from what I had anticipated.

Over the course of my trip, I traveled to several cities and towns, speaking with locals and immersing myself in their daily lives. I visited a number of historical sites, such as the Apartheid Museum and the Hector Pieterson Memorial, both of which provided a stark reminder of the country's troubled past. However, I was also struck by the resilience and hope of the people I met, who had overcome unimaginable obstacles to build a new, more inclusive society.

As I navigated the country, I learned a great deal about myself. I came to appreciate the value of stepping outside of my comfort zone and embracing new experiences. I learned to trust my instincts and embrace uncertainty, even when it felt uncomfortable or scary. I discovered a newfound sense of courage and self-reliance, as I navigated unfamiliar streets and interacted with strangers in a foreign language.

Of course, there were obstacles along the way. At times, I felt lost and overwhelmed, unsure of how to navigate the complexities of this new culture. I encountered language barriers and cultural misunderstandings, and I struggled with feelings of homesickness and loneliness. However, as I pushed through these challenges, I gained strength and resilience, emerging from the experience with a newfound sense of confidence and self-assurance.

Looking back on my trip to South Africa, I am incredibly grateful for the lessons I learned and the experiences I had. I will always remember the bright colors and smells of the local markets, the sound of drumming at a traditional Zulu ceremony, and the feel of the warm sand beneath my feet as I walked along a pristine beach. Another challenge I faced was navigating unfamiliar transportation systems. Buses and taxis in South Africa can be confusing and intimidating, especially for someone who is used to driving or taking trains. I had to learn how to read maps, decipher schedules, and ask for help when I needed it.

content:Speaker assistant says: Museums can overcome the disadvantage of reducing visitors due to admission fees by implementing other ways of raising funds. Additionally, museums could establish partnerships with businesses or government agencies to help cover their costs. content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Here are a few additional examples of fundraising events that museums could organize to raise their funds:

1. Walkathons or Fun Runs - These events are becoming increasingly popular and can be a great way to raise funds while also promoting health and wellness. Participants can walk or run on a designated course around the museum or in a nearby park, while seeking sponsorships from friends and family members.

2. Art Exhibitions and Sales - Museums could partner with local artists or galleries to display and sell artwork related to a particular exhibit or theme. A portion of the proceeds from each sale could be donated to the museum.

3. Workshops and Classes - Museums could offer paid workshops or classes related to their exhibits or collections. For example, a natural history museum could offer a class on fossil hunting, while an art museum could offer a workshop on painting techniques. The fees charged for these events could go towards the museum's operations and programming.

4. Benefit Concerts - Museums could organize benefit concerts featuring local or national musicians, with ticket sales going towards the museum's fundraising efforts. These events could be held in the museum's courtyard or in another suitable outdoor venue.

content:Speaker assistant says: The economic motivations behind British colonialism during the 16th to 19th centuries were primarily driven by the desire to gain self-sufficiency and access to valuable resources. The British sought colonies that could provide them with precious metals, raw materials, and convenient markets to sell their manufactured products.

Trade was the most powerful motivation for British colonialism. British traders and merchants wanted to expand their businesses and gain access to new markets. They established trading posts and routes around the world to get the goods they needed or to sell their own goods. They also created monopolies on certain products or industries, such as the British East India Company's monopoly on trade with India.

As British colonialism expanded into more territories, taxation and administration became important tools for controlling the colonies. While British colonies were allowed to have their own legislative bodies, they still faced restrictions on their trade and governance. The British also imposed taxes on the colonies to pay for the costs of administering them.

These economic motivations impacted the colonies in varying ways. Some colonies, such as those in North America, became prosperous through their trade with the British Empire. Others, such as those in Africa and Asia, were exploited for their natural resources without receiving much in return. Some colonies were used as penal colonies, such as Australia, or as places for British emigrants to settle, such as in Canada.

The exploitative economic practices of colonialism often led to poverty, inequality, and environmental destruction in the colonies. Some British colonial policies also exacerbated conflict and tension between different ethnic and religious groups within the colonies, leading to problems that persist until today.

Overall, the economic motivations behind British colonialism played a significant role in shaping the colonies and their relationship with the British Empire. While British colonialism had some positive impacts on the colonies, it also had many negative consequences that continue to be felt today. context:British colonialism in the 16th-19th centuries was primarily fueled by the desire for self-sufficiency through access to valuable resources, particularly through trade and the exploitation of resources and markets, leading to significant economic and social consequences. keywords: colonialism, economic motivations, trade tags: economics, colonialism, history
